title: NFA
body:
**Nondeterministic Finite Automaton.** A [[DFA]] with the determinism requirement dropped: a
state may have several transitions on the same symbol, none at all, or transitions that
consume nothing.

## Formal definition

$N = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$, identical to a [[DFA]] except for $\delta$:

$$\delta: Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \to \mathcal{P}(Q)$$

It returns a *set* of states rather than one state, and it accepts $\varepsilon$ as an input
symbol. Those two changes are the entire difference. $\emptyset$ is a legal result, which is
how "no transition" is expressed.

## How acceptance works

An NFA accepts $w$ if **some** path through the machine ends in an accepting state. Not all
paths, some. Dead ends do not matter as long as one branch survives.

Two ways to think about it, and both appear in the course:

- **Guessing**: the machine magically picks the right transition whenever there is a choice.
- **Parallel**: the machine is in a *set* of states at once, and after each symbol you compute
  the set of states reachable from all of them.

The parallel reading is the honest one, and it is also the [[Simulation|simulation]] algorithm
and the proof of the theorem below.

## $\varepsilon$-transitions

An $\varepsilon$-move changes state without reading a symbol. It is glue: it lets you wire two
machines together for union or concatenation without rewriting either. The
$\varepsilon$-closure of a state is every state reachable from it by $\varepsilon$-moves alone,
including itself, and every NFA algorithm starts by taking one.

## The subset construction

> Every NFA has an equivalent DFA.

The proof is a construction, and it is the exam question. Make each DFA state a **subset** of
the NFA's states:

- DFA start state = $\varepsilon$-closure of $\{q_0\}$
- $\delta_D(S, a) = \varepsilon\text{-closure}\big(\bigcup_{q \in S} \delta_N(q, a)\big)$
- a DFA state is accepting if the subset contains any NFA accepting state

$Q$ has $n$ states, so there are $2^n$ subsets, and the DFA can need all of them. Exponential
in the *worst* case; in practice most subsets are unreachable and you only build the ones you
hit.

```
NFA over {a,b}: strings whose second-last symbol is a
  q0 --a,b--> q0,  q0 --a--> q1,  q1 --a,b--> q2 (accepting)

subsets reached: {q0}, {q0,q1}, {q0,q2}, {q0,q1,q2}
4 states, which is 2^2 of the non-start states. Not a coincidence.
```

The consequence is the important part: **nondeterminism gives a finite automaton no extra
power.** NFAs and DFAs recognise exactly the same class, the [[Regular Languages]]. An NFA is
a convenience, never a capability.

That is not a general law. It happens again for [[Turing Machine]]s and it *fails* for
[[Pushdown Automata]], where a nondeterministic PDA is strictly stronger than a deterministic
one. See [[Nondeterminism]] for the pattern across all three.

## Why bother

- NFAs are far smaller and easier to draw. "Contains `abb` somewhere" is three states plus a
  self-loop instead of a table you have to think about.
- The conversion from [[Regular Expressions]] (Thompson's construction) produces an NFA
  directly, one small gadget per operator, glued with $\varepsilon$-moves.
- Real tools do exactly this: regex → NFA → DFA → transition table.

## Core Facts to Know

- $\delta: Q \times (\Sigma \cup \{\varepsilon\}) \to \mathcal{P}(Q)$, returning a set of states.
- A state may have zero, one, or many transitions on a symbol.
- $\varepsilon$-transitions move without consuming input.
- The NFA accepts if **at least one** computation path ends in an accepting state.
- Every NFA has an equivalent [[DFA]] via the **subset construction**.
- DFA states are subsets of NFA states, so up to $2^n$ of them.
- Nondeterminism adds no power to a finite automaton, only brevity.
- Nondeterminism *does* add power to a [[Pushdown Automata|PDA]], and does *not* to a [[Turing Machine]].
- NFAs are what regular expressions compile to, which is why the equivalence matters in practice.
- You cannot complement an NFA by swapping accepting states; convert to a DFA first.
